a1_porch.title: The Last House on Marrow Street
a1_porch.text: The door opens before your knuckles reach it, which is rude of it, or generous. "Trick or treat," you say, because that is what you say. "Which?" asks a polite voice from the warm dark inside. It has been waiting a long time to be polite to someone.{{#if visits>0}} The door does not trouble to check who you are.{{#if last_ending}} It swings a little wider than it needs to, for someone it has met before.{{/if}}{{/if}} Behind the voice, the hallway goes back further than the house is wide. Your friends wait under the lamp at the corner. At your feet grins a jack-o'-lantern nobody on Marrow Street remembers carving.

a1_treat_hand.title: A Gloved Hand
a1_treat_hand.text:
A gloved hand comes out of the warm and drops three sweets into your bag, one at a time, each with the soft sound of a coin going into velvet. They are wrapped in waxed paper twisted at both ends, and they are warm.

"Lovely," says the voice. Somewhere deeper in, a pen scratches one short line. Then the hand turns over, palm up, patient as a collection plate. "May I take your coat?"

a1_trick_laugh.title: Delight
a1_trick_laugh.text:
For a moment there is no sound from inside at all. Then laughter: a boy's laugh coming out of a gentleman's throat, high and helpless, from someone who has not heard that answer in a very long time.

"Trick," says the voice, tasting it. "Oh, well done. Then you'd better come in and play it. Our visitor leads, one to nothing." Nobody holds the door. Nobody bars it. On the rail sits a bowl of sweets, unattended. The jack-o'-lantern's candle burns on the step, plainer than the porch light, and behind you the path runs down to the gate.

a1_trick_porch.title: Light Fingers
a1_trick_porch.text:
Your host watches from the doorway, a short figure with gloved hands folded. "A point to our visitor," he says, with real pleasure.{{#if candle}} Behind you the jack-o'-lantern has gone dark, its grin only a hole cut in a vegetable. The candle in your hand burns small and steady, and by its light the hallway is exactly as long as the house is wide.{{/if}}{{#if candy>=2}} The sweets from the bowl are still warm in your pocket.{{/if}}

The door stays open. Nobody has asked it to close in a very long time. Down at the gate the path is still there, and so, for now, is the street.

a1_trick_path.title: The Path Back
a1_trick_path.text:
Halfway down the path you look back once. The door is still open and the porch light still on, warm air pouring out into the cold. The house would sooner heat the whole street than shut its door on you.{{#if candle}} The candle in your hand leans back toward the house.{{/if}}{{#if candy>=2}} The stolen sweets drag at your pocket, heavier than sweets ought to be.{{/if}}

A fine rain starts. Your friends are at the corner, arguing about whose turn it is. Nobody calls you back. Nobody calls you anything.

a1_name.title: The Threshold
a1_name.text:
{{#if stance=treat}}{{#if candy>=4}}A fourth sweet drops into your bag. "Lovely," the voice says again, and deeper in, the pen scratches a second line.{{else}}{{#if debt>=2}}The gloved hand takes your coat into the warm, and it goes away from you down the hall to the hooks.{{else}}The gloved hand lets itself fall, not in the least offended.{{/if}}{{/if}}{{else}}You come in out of the cold, as far as the doormat.{{#if candy>=1}} The porch sweets rustle in your pocket.{{/if}}{{/if}} Your host stands just inside, beyond a brass threshold worn bright by a great many feet. He is smaller than his voice: an evening coat whose tails brush the floor, white gloves a size too large, a moustache drawn on in burnt cork.{{#if candle}} By the candle his gloves are the colour of very old paper.{{/if}}{{#if stance=treat}} Behind you, the top step has quietly become the bottom of a long hill.{{/if}}

"Call me Mr. Marrow." He bows. {{#if stance=treat}}"And whom do I have the pleasure of, my guest?"{{else}}"And whom shall I say is visiting?"{{/if}} Down the hall, a row of coats stirs on their hooks, listening.

a1_foyer.title: The Foyer

a1_push.title: First Through the Door
a1_push.text:
You shoulder past him. He flattens himself against the frame before you can touch him, and the glove you brush weighs almost nothing. Then he laughs, delighted. You have gone first, and spared him the asking. He follows you in, which suits him very well. "A point to our visitor."

The foyer is gold and very warm. Three portraits on the far wall have their eyes painted out.{{#if candle}} By your candle it is only paint.{{/if}} Brass hooks along the near wall are tagged 1898, 1931, 1953, 1979. Every clock in the room says 11:59, and none of them moves. Under the floor something knocks once, and stops.

"Did anyone see you come up the path?" he asks, lightly.

a1_riddle.title: A Small Game

end_no_one_home.title: No One Home
end_no_one_home.text:
You do not look round.{{#if candle}} Behind you, though you never see it, the pumpkin on the step stays dark.{{/if}} At the corner your friends want to know what took so long, and you find you have nothing at all to tell them.{{#if candy>=1}} The stolen sweets sit in a drawer for years. You never eat them, and you never quite throw them away.{{/if}}

You grow up. You have a front door of your own, with a good lock. And every Halloween, at one minute to midnight, it swings open by itself and lets the warm out into the dark, politely, though nobody has knocked. Every year you get up and shut it. Every year it asks again.

ending.title: No One Home
ending.epitaph: Declined, with thanks. The door still asks.

a2_hub.title: Three Doors

choices.label: Follow the smell to the kitchen

a2_hub_2.title: Two Doors
a2_hub_2.text:
The parlor doors shut behind you, and the fire's heat stays in your hands a little way down the passage. {{#if clock}}Behind the doors the tall clock ticks for the first time in a hundred and twenty-eight years. It still says 11:59, and every clock in the foyer has noticed: one of them has begun to hum.{{else}}The little brass key swings on your host's chain among the fobs.{{/if}}

From the passage comes the smell of supper. Where the wall beside the stair was solid, an arch of ivy now lets out the green light. Your host's glance says you will get one of them, not both.{{#if name_given}} On the hooks by the door, one empty hook is swinging.{{/if}}{{#if stance=treat}}{{#unless debt>=1}} Your host looks at your empty hands and very pointedly does not say "Lovely."{{/unless}}{{/if}}

choices.label: Follow the smell to the kitchen

a2_hub_stair.title: The Stair

a2_parlor_book.title: The Guestbook
a2_parlor_book.text:
Your host opens the parlor doors and stands flat to the frame. "After you." Inside: a real fire, the family over the mantel with their eyes painted out, and a guestbook lying open on a stand.

The first line, where a host would sign before any guest, is blank. Under it is a line in a boy's careful capitals, dated 1898. After that the names grow larger and less steady with every year: Hester Vane, 1931. Philippa Ashdown, 1953. {{#if name_given}}Below the newest name there is a space exactly your size.{{/if}}{{#if stance=treat}} "The pen is just there, my guest," says your host.{{/if}}

a2_parlor_pages.title: The First Page
a2_parlor_pages.text:
You turn back, leaf by leaf, to 1898. The host's line is blank. Under it, in a boy's careful capitals, one word can still be read: EDWIN. The rest of the line is gone under a gloved thumbprint, pressed there while the ink was wet.

After that, one line for each Halloween, and some Halloweens nobody at all. The hands grow larger and less steady: Hester Vane, 1931, in a round kitchen hand. Philippa Ashdown, 1953. D. Okafor, 1979. Behind you your host has stopped talking. When you look round, his moustache has smudged at one corner, and he is watching the fire.

a2_parlor_fire.title: The Stopped Clock
a2_parlor_fire.text:
The guestbook shuts with a soft clap of old paper.

The fire is the best fire you have ever stood near. In the corner a tall clock says one minute to midnight, its pendulum hanging dead still behind the glass. There is a keyhole low on the dial. The key is on your host's watch chain, a small brass thing among the fobs. {{#if stance=treat}}"Is there anything you need, my guest?" he asks, and for once he seems to hope there is not.{{else}}He lets the chain swing where you can see it.{{/if}}

choices.label: Lift the key from his chain

a2_parlor_false.title: A False Name
a2_parlor_false.text:
You write a name that is not yours, and the ink takes it without complaint. Your host reads it upside down.{{#if lies=1}} "Ah."{{#if debt>=1}} He lifts the pen off the stand. "Then we are playing after all, and you are our visitor. You won't need this."{{/if}}{{else}} He does not say "Ah." He draws one short stroke in the margin for each story you have told him tonight.{{/if}}

In the corner a tall clock says one minute to midnight, its pendulum dead still behind the glass. There is a keyhole low on the dial. The key that fits it is a small brass thing among the fobs on your host's watch chain, and he lets the chain swing where you can see it.

choices.label: Lift the key from his chain

a2_parlor_clock.title: The Key
a2_parlor_clock.text:
{{#if stance=treat}}He unhooks the key with a small sigh he does not let himself finish, and closes your fingers over it with both gloves. "Lovely."{{else}}The chain swings out on his next gesture, and the key comes away in your fingers. He watches it go, and lets it.{{/if}} The key is warm from his waistcoat.

Wound, the clock could strike midnight. It has not been allowed to in a hundred and twenty-eight years. Your host says nothing at all, which is the loudest thing he has done tonight.{{#if lied}} He watches the clock, not you.{{/if}}

a2_parlor_leave.title: Settling Up
a2_parlor_leave.text:
You leave the little key on its chain, and the clock goes on saying one minute to midnight. Your host opens the guestbook again at a narrow column you had taken for a margin, headed in faded copperplate: Received.

{{#if debt>=1}}Under it, in his careful capitals, are your entries.{{#if debt=6}} There are six lines: the sweets at the door, and five gifts since.{{else}}{{#if debt=5}} There are five lines: the sweets at the door, and four gifts since.{{else}}{{#if debt=4}} There are four lines: the sweets at the door, and three gifts since.{{else}}{{#if debt=3}} There are three lines: the sweets at the door, and two gifts since.{{else}}{{#if debt=2}} There are two lines: the sweets at the door, and one gift since.{{else}}{{#if debt=1}} There is a single line: the sweets at the door.{{/if}}{{/if}}{{/if}}{{/if}}{{/if}}{{/if}} "Sweets settle it," he says, uncapping the pen. "One strikes one. A clean page at midnight is a guest let go, if midnight ever came." He holds the nib over the column and looks, of all things, sorry.{{else}}Under it there is nothing of yours at all. "Our visitor owes the house nothing," he says, and bows you toward the doors. Behind him the fire burns on for nobody.{{/if}} Over the mantel, the painted family waits for you to go.

choices.label: Warm your hands at his fire

a2_kitchen_door.title: The Cook
a2_kitchen_door.text:
The kitchen is the warmest room yet: copper pans, a black range, herbs hanging from the beams like bats asleep. A woman in a tea-towel turban is wiping her hands on her apron. They are perfectly clean. She hums three bars of the waltz, stops, and counts spoons.

{{#if stance=treat}}"Sit yourself down, duck," she says, pulling out the one chair at a feast laid for one. "Cook will do."{{else}}"I don't serve strangers," she tells the wall, and keeps her back to you. The stove behind her is crowded and unguarded.{{/if}}{{#if ledger}} You know her name. It was in the guestbook, in a round kitchen hand: Hester Vane, 1931.{{/if}} She wipes her clean hands again. "I came as a fortune-teller, you know. Yours is a short one."

a2_kitchen_thanks.title: Hester

a2_kitchen_feast.title: Seconds
a2_kitchen_feast.text:
It is the best thing you have ever tasted: new bread, a clove or two, something slow that has been on the stove since before you were born. You try to picture your front door, and cannot say what colour it is. That does not seem to matter much.{{#if stance=treat}} Down the passage, someone says "Lovely."{{/if}} When you have finished, the wishbone from the saucer is in your pocket.

{{#if stance=trick}}{{#if ledger}}Hester has turned round for the first time.{{else}}The cook has turned round for the first time.{{/if}}{{/if}} Her ladle stops halfway to the pot. "I'll tell you plainly, because nobody told me," she says. "One helping is a meal. Two is a job." A clean tea towel lies folded on the dresser, put out ready.

a2_kitchen_bone.title: The Wishbone
a2_kitchen_bone.text:
{{#if stance=treat}}She takes your hand and reads it by the light of the range. "It's all about supper," she says.{{else}}She does not turn round, for a question or for a hand in her pans. "Your fortune, since you're in my kitchen," she tells the wall.{{/if}} "Whoever eats here forgets the way home. That's the whole of it. It's very good food." She says the last part as an apology.

On a saucer by the range a wishbone is drying, small and clean, the forked kind you pull to make a wish. {{#if stance=treat}}"Take it, duck. A present." Down the passage, a pen lifts.{{else}}Her back stays turned. Behind her the pot simmers, smelling of every supper you ever came in to out of the dark.{{/if}}

a2_kitchen_floor.title: Under the Flagstones
a2_kitchen_floor.text:
{{#if fed}}She clears away after your supper without a word.{{else}}{{#if wishbone}}The wishbone sits light in your pocket.{{else}}You leave the wishbone on its saucer, and she nods once.{{/if}}{{/if}} Then three knocks come up through the flagstones, slow and polite, close enough to feel in your heels. {{#if ledger}}Hester goes white and grips a spoon.{{else}}The cook goes white and grips a spoon.{{/if}}

"Don't you go answering that," she says. "Every knock you give back is asking. Three, and it comes up to meet you. All my years here I've never answered, and I still don't know what it wants. Nobody's ever asked it." The flagstone under you is warm as a loaf under a cloth, and sits a little proud of the others.{{#if fed}} You find you would quite like to knock back. It seems only polite.{{/if}}

a2_cons_door.title: Dez

choices.label: Ask how he fools the house

a2_cons_lesson.title: The Lie Trick
a2_cons_lesson.text:
Dez grins. "It can't call a lie a lie, man. It's too polite." He taps the dish twice. "Whatever you tell it, it has to take your word."

{{#if stance=treat}}He taps again, twice, and the grin goes. "But a guest who lies stops being a guest. Then nothing in here has to be nice to you."{{else}}He leans closer. "Next time the old man asks you something, give him the answer you'd like to be true. He'll thank you for it."{{/if}}{{#if lied}} He squints at you. "You already did it, didn't you. Natural."{{/if}} The vines creep closer to listen. He holds the light out to you again.

a2_cons_out.title: Find Anything
a2_cons_out.text:
{{#if stance=treat}}{{#if candle}}"Say it," Dez tells you, and you say it: no more eating in this house. He taps the dish twice and puts the candle in your hands. Then he goes out among the vines like a pinched wick, and the last of him looks relieved.{{else}}"Suit yourself, man," says Dez, and keeps his light.{{/if}}{{else}}Dez's last word follows you out, low and cheerful: "Outstanding." The vines close over the place where he was sitting.{{#if candle}} The flame in your hand is a single flame, and always was.{{/if}}{{/if}}

Your host is waiting just past the sill. Nobody ever asked him in.{{#if candle}} He does not look at the candle, very carefully.{{/if}}{{#if lied}} He has the pen uncapped before you have said a word.{{/if}} "Find anything, in there?" He asks it lightly. He asked about the path lightly, too. He waits to write down whatever you say.

a2_cons_lie.title: Only Vines

end_seconds.title: Seconds
end_seconds.text:
You were warned, and you hold out your plate anyway. {{#if stance=trick}}She takes it from you and looks you properly in the face.{{/if}} {{#if ledger}}Hester smiles for the first time since 1931.{{else}}The cook smiles for the first time since 1931.{{/if}} She fills the plate, sets it down, and hands you the tea towel.

Then she unties her apron, sits in the chair by the range, and closes her eyes. The spoons want counting. Out in the foyer the front door is opening for someone new, and you find you already know what they will want for supper.

ending.title: Seconds
ending.epitaph: There was always room for more.

a3_hall.title: The Upstairs Hall
a3_hall.text:
{{#if candle}}You come up behind the candle, and by its light the portraits are only paint. You stand in a hall exactly the width of the house.{{else}}The sweet tastes of cloves. While you chew, the hall shortens, door by door, until it is exactly the width of the house.{{/if}}{{#if fed}} The runner is soft underfoot, softer than carpet should be. When you look back, the stair is gone, and you do not mind.{{/if}}{{#if riddle=right}} A clock on the landing reads 11:59. You knew that before you looked.{{/if}}

{{#if name_given}}The nearer door has a name painted on it in a child's careful capitals.{{#if name}} It says {{name}}.{{/if}} Cold comes under the farther door, the flat cold of glass. The attic steps wait at the far end, and the hall, politely, will not let you that far yet.{{else}}The nearer door has no handle, only a smooth place where a handle would go. Cold comes under the farther door, the flat cold of glass. With one door fewer to offer, the hall lets you reach the attic steps at its far end.{{/if}}

a3_hall_long.title: The Long Hall
a3_hall_long.text:
The hall goes on longer than the house is wide. Portraits, doors, a red runner worn pale down the middle, candles burning without a tremor. You count twelve doors and stop counting. When you look back, the stair has gone and there is only more hall. Your host is nowhere in it, though he would come if called. He is that kind of host.

{{#if name_given}}Somewhere ahead the house is trying out your name under its breath, getting the vowels right.{{#if name}} "{{name}}," it says at last, a little too carefully.{{/if}}{{/if}}{{#if candy>=1}} Your bag rustles. The sweets in it are warm through the paper. One would give your hands something to do.{{/if}}

choices.label: Eat a sweet to steady yourself

a3_hall_dark.title: The Same Hall
a3_hall_dark.text:
The same hall. The same runner, the same candles, the same twelve doors. In the first portrait the man's evening coat is not an evening coat any more. It is yours, down to the pulled thread at the cuff.

{{#if name_given}}Behind you, quite close, someone says your name, fondly, from across a room that is not there.{{#if name}} "{{name}}," it says again, and this time it has the vowels exactly right.{{/if}} You turn, and two doors are at your elbow. They have been there all along.{{else}}{{#if stance=treat}}Something takes you by the shoulders, gently, turns you out of the wrong room, and sets you down in front of two doors, with the attic steps just beyond them.{{else}}Nothing turns you round. Two doors stand at your elbow, the attic steps climb beyond them, and ahead, past the last candle, the dark holds its own door open.{{/if}}{{/if}}{{#if stance=trick}}{{#if fear>=8}} Past the last candle the dark looks restful. Nobody has put anything in its way.{{/if}}{{/if}}

a3_hall_arm.title: His Arm

a3_hall_2.title: Two Doors Left

a3_nursery_door.title: The Nursery
a3_nursery_door.text:
The room is new. The paint smells new, the moon in the window is too round, and the crib is exactly your size. It was made the moment you gave your name.

Someone is in it already: a girl in a bedsheet ghost, the eyeholes cut crooked, one higher than the other. {{#if stance=treat}}"You're a guest too," she whispers. "Don't take anything else off him. He's nice. That's how he does it."{{else}}She peers at you through the lower eyehole.{{#if lied}}{{#if lies>=2}} "You've been fibbing to him all night," she says, delighted.{{else}} "You've been fibbing to him," she says, delighted.{{/if}} "I can tell. He's gone all polite with you. Good. Somebody has to."{{else}} "You didn't say treat," she says, delighted. "Good. Somebody has to."{{/if}}{{/if}}{{#if candle}} Where the candle shines through the eyeholes there is nothing behind them, and the sheet stands up anyway.{{/if}}

a3_nursery_pip.title: Is It Still Halloween

a3_nursery_year.title: Seventy-Three

a3_nursery_window.title: Her Porch Light
a3_nursery_window.text:
{{#if knocks>=2}}The wall answers your knock once, softer, and waits. A question, this time. {{/if}}Pip takes your answer to the window with her and kneels on a chair, eyeholes to the glass. "There. Past the lamp." {{#if fed}}Where she looks you see only a soft grey nothing, with nothing written on it yet. Her face, through the sheet, is turned toward it and shining.{{else}}At the bottom of a street that runs on further than any street should is a porch light in a little iron cage. It is on.{{/if}}

"She always leaves it on till the last one's in." {{#if trust=1}}She winds a ribbon round her fingers and does not hold it out. Not yet.{{else}}{{#if trust<=-2}}She turns from you to the wall and says, quite clearly, "They're in here." Somewhere in the house a pen moves.{{else}}She keeps her hands on the glass.{{/if}}{{/if}}

a3_nursery_stay.title: A While

a3_mirror_door.title: The Other Guest
a3_mirror_door.text:
A room that is all mirror, every wall and the back of the door, and the glass is perfectly steady. The candles in it do not flicker. {{#if fed}}Where you should be, the glass shows a front door with a brass number and a worn mat. It is yours. You could not have said so a minute ago.{{else}}Your reflection lifts its hand half a second after you. Then, having decided something, half a second before.{{/if}}

{{#if stance=treat}}"I'd only like a word," it says, in your voice, wheedling. "You'd be doing me a kindness."{{else}}"Go on, then," it says, in your voice. "You first. Or me. Let's see who's quicker."{{/if}} It lets that settle.{{#if riddle=right}} "I knew the answer too, downstairs. The clock. I'm you, after all."{{else}} "I guessed the same as you, downstairs. I'm you, after all."{{/if}}{{#if endings_found>=2}} Then, nearly kind: "We've had this talk before. You never remember it. I do."{{/if}}

a3_mirror_offer.title: The Trade
a3_mirror_offer.text:
It speaks first, before you have finished deciding to listen. {{#if fed}}The front door in the glass stays put the whole time, and only the voice is yours.{{else}}Your reflection lays its palm flat on the inside of the glass, and the glass does not shiver.{{/if}}

"Here's the offer," it says, plainly. It is not the house, and it has no need to be polite. "Let me keep your reflection. The house counts heads, not faces, so it will count one of us as staying, and you can go. The price is your face. You never see it again: not in glass, not in water, not in a dark window, not in a spoon." {{#if ribbon}}It has noticed the ribbon at your pocket. "Or one of us could stay in her place. Think about that."{{/if}}

a3_mirror_back.title: Your Back
a3_mirror_back.text:
You turn round.{{#if fed}} No wall shows any of you. In the glass of the door your own front door waits, and the voice comes out of it.{{else}} Every wall shows you the back of your own head, the collar, the parting in your hair, all of it half a second late. Only the glass in the door shows your face, and your face is watching you.{{/if}}

"Suit yourself," it says to the back of your head. "I'll be quick, then. The house counts heads, not faces. Let me keep your reflection and it counts one of us as staying, and you can go. The price is your face, for good.{{#if ribbon}} Or one of us could stay in her place. Think about that.{{/if}} You'd have to turn round to say yes."

a3_mirror_no.title: No

choices.label: Give it your reflection after all
Give it your reflection after all

a3_attic_stair.title: The Trunks
a3_attic_stair.text:
{{#if mirror}}Behind you your reflection says "Thank you" in your voice, and the next window you pass has nobody in it.{{else}}Nobody follows you up.{{/if}} The attic steps climb into rain on the roof. Trunks stand along the eaves, each with a year chalked on the lid: 1931, 1953, 1979, dozens more.

The oldest says 1898: a boy's Sunday clothes, a burnt cork, and a coat-shaped gap where something was folded and never put back, because he is still wearing it. A paper tag is pinned inside the lid. {{#unless candle}}{{#if ledger}}You know that hand from the guestbook's 1898 line.{{else}}In the house's light it is a smudge of careful capitals.{{/if}}{{/unless}}{{#unless name_given}} Under the boards a girl's voice says, "I can't come up. There isn't a room for me. Is it still Halloween out there?"{{/unless}}

choices.label: Match the hand to the guestbook

a3_attic_floor.title: Rain on the Roof
a3_attic_floor.text:
{{#if true_name}}You unpin the tag.{{#if candle}} You read it by the flame.{{else}} It is the same hand as the guestbook's 1898 line.{{/if}} EDWIN A. TULL, AGE 11, printed very clearly by a boy who was told to. You put it in your pocket. Your host has a name. It weighs almost nothing.{{else}}The coat-shaped gap stays where it is. Rain goes over the roof like someone counting coins.{{/if}}{{#unless name_given}}{{#if trust>=1}} Under the boards the girl has gone quiet. Then, very small: "That's not an hour."{{/if}}{{/unless}}

Three knocks come up through the floor, from a place that should not be above anything.{{#if knocks>=1}} Warm air and cloves rise between the boards, and a girl's voice says, "Welcome."{{/if}} Then nothing. The floor is waiting to hear whether you are in.

a3_hatch.title: The Hatch

end_lights_out.title: Lights Out
end_lights_out.text:
You walk past the last candle, and nobody stops you, because nobody has to. The dark gives you exactly what you are owed: no doors, no runner, no portraits to count, no end. Behind you the hall is a small square of light that does not get any smaller.

Then it does. You keep walking. It is easy, after a while. Somewhere far back a coat hangs on a hook that was not there before, and the house, which never lies, does not mention you again.

ending.title: Lights Out
ending.epitaph: Walked the hall. The hall walked further.

a4_cellar.title: The Cellar

a4_jars.title: The Jars
a4_jars.text:
Every jar has a paper label tied round its neck in careful capitals: a date and a street. *OCT. 31, 1931. ORCHARD LANE.* Inside each, very small, something goes round and round the glass. A screen door. A mother calling a name across a garden at dusk.

One jar from 1953 is different. It holds sweets in waxed paper, twisted at both ends, never spent.{{#if trust>=1}} The sheet at your elbow goes very still. "Those are mine," it whispers. "For when I get home."{{/if}}{{#if fed}} At the end of the shelf stands a new jar, its lid still bright. The label is a street you do not recognise, and you are sure you should.{{/if}}

a4_jars_sweets.title: Nineteen Fifty-Three

a4_door.title: The Green Door
a4_door.text:
You leave the shelves behind. The roots end at a door painted the green of a front door on a good street, with a brass plate, a handle, and no keyhole.{{#if candle}} By your candle the green is only paint on brick, and through it you can see a long table, laid.{{/if}}{{#if knocks>=3}} Your hand goes flat on the warm paint. You have answered three times tonight, and the count is already whole. Whatever is behind the door is on its way up to meet you.{{else}}{{#if knocks>=2}} Your hand goes flat on the warm paint. You have answered it twice tonight. Answer once more and the count is whole: it will come up to meet you. Nobody has ever asked it what it wants.{{/if}}{{/if}}

From the other side, low down, comes a knock. Then another. Then a third, and then the patient nothing of someone waiting on a step, because it is always 11:59.

a4_table.title: The Long Table

choices.label: Leave the book as it is

a4_table_book.title: The Green Book
a4_table_book.text:
Mr. Marrow turns the green book to face you.{{#if debt=1}} There is a single stroke on your page.{{else}}{{#if debt=2}} There are two strokes on your page.{{else}}{{#if debt=3}} There are three strokes on your page.{{else}}{{#if debt=4}} There are four strokes on your page.{{else}}{{#if debt=5}} There are five strokes on your page.{{else}}{{#if debt>=6}} There are six strokes on your page.{{/if}}{{/if}}{{/if}}{{/if}}{{/if}}{{/if}} Each is a kindness you said yes to, entered the moment you said it. He uncaps the pen. "Sweets settle it. One strikes one."

He is honest about the rest, because he has to be.{{#if stance=trick}} "A visitor's page, settled, is still a visitor's page. It will not make you a guest again."{{else}} "Settling keeps a guest's page clean. Whether a clean page is let out is midnight's business."{{#unless clock}} He glances at the stopped clocks. "And midnight is not coming tonight."{{/unless}}{{/if}}

a4_gate.title: The Final Gate
a4_gate.text:
Mr. Marrow closes the green book.{{#if debt>=1}} Something is still owing.{{else}} Your page is clean.{{/if}}{{#if fed}} You can still taste the plate.{{/if}} From under the cloth the Marrow speaks its one word. "Welcome." It uses your voice.{{#if endings_found>=3}} It has had practice.{{/if}} It wears it carefully, like borrowed shoes.

What you carry is what you have.{{#if mirror}} In the glasses along the table, nobody stands where you stand.{{/if}}{{#if clock}} Behind Mr. Marrow the clock is ticking.{{/if}}{{#if candle}} The honest flame stands straight.{{#if fed}}{{#if stance=treat}} It gutters once, for what you promised Dez.{{/if}}{{/if}}{{else}}{{#unless clock}}{{#unless true_name}} You came down without a light, an hour, or his name.{{/unless}}{{/unless}}{{/if}}{{#if wishbone}} The wishbone in your pocket has gone warm.{{/if}}{{#if ribbon}} The ribbon tugs twice: Pip, checking you are there.{{/if}}{{#if stance=treat}}{{#unless debt>=1}}{{#unless clock}} "You have been a very good guest," he says. It is not a compliment.{{/unless}}{{/unless}}{{/if}} He pulls out your chair, and waits.

a4_gate_name.title: Edwin Ashby Tull
a4_gate_name.text:
"Edwin A. Tull," you say.

It goes into the room like a stone into a well. "Ashby," he says, and for a moment he is not Mr. Marrow but a boy of eleven in his dead father's coat. He wipes his mouth, and the moustache smears. "Edwin Ashby Tull. Yes."{{#if stance=treat}} Not "Lovely." Only yes.{{else}}{{#if debt>=1}} Not "Lovely." Only yes.{{else}} Only yes.{{/if}}{{/if}} "One question, or one order. Make it something good."{{#if fed}} You have eaten at his table. If he opened every door in the house, you would not know which was yours.{{else}} You have eaten nothing here, and still know the way home, if someone would only open the door.{{/if}}{{#if ledger}} You think of the guestbook's blank first line, where a host would sign.{{/if}}{{#if wishbone}} The wishbone in your pocket is warm.{{/if}}{{#if knocks>=3}} Under the cloth something is waiting for a knock it cannot start itself.{{/if}}

a4_gate_light.title: The Honest Flame
a4_gate_light.text:
You hold up the candle, and the Marrow shrinks to its real size. The table is a plank on trestles, twenty places perhaps, and the chandeliers are only roots. The stillnesses are coats over chair-backs. At the far end, painted to look like brick, is a door.{{#if ribbon}} Pip is beside you. Under the flame her sheet is empty, and the ribbon is still held at the other end.{{/if}}{{#if mirror}} Near the foot of the table someone with your face is already sitting down.{{/if}}

Mr. Marrow shades his eyes. "Not one of ours, that," he says, and does not ask you to put it out.{{#if stance=treat}} "A guest leaves by the front door, at the proper hour. The flame is for strangers."{{/if}}

a4_gate_midnight.title: Midnight

a4_gate_seat.title: Your Seat
a4_gate_seat.text: Your place card. Your chair. It is warm, and it takes you all at once. Mr. Marrow pushes it in and lays the napkin in your lap. He is waiting to see what you have brought to the table.{{#if fed}} You have eaten in this house already, and your plate knows it.{{else}} You have eaten nothing here, and the lid is still on your plate.{{/if}}{{#if knocks>=3}} Under your feet there is a hatch, and something on the other side is waiting very politely to be let up.{{/if}} At his elbow the green book lies open at the back page, where bills are kept. Behind you the cellar is dark and long, and nobody is guarding it.

end_housewarming.title: Housewarming
end_housewarming.text:
"Fetch the guestbook," you tell him, by his name, and Edwin brings it. The host's line is blank. You knock a fourth time, on the table, the first knock anyone has ever started from this side. You snap the wishbone, wish the house a name of its own, and write it there in the host's place. *Marrow.*

The hunger has a name and something to be. The room cools. Hester unties her apron. Upstairs, a candle you never saw goes out.{{#if name_given}} A sheet with crooked eyeholes runs for the stair.{{/if}} Edwin is eleven for one second, then dust in a good coat. You walk out the front door into an ordinary morning, and only you remember them.{{#if stance=treat}} Nobody says "Lovely."{{else}}{{#if debt>=1}} Nobody says "Lovely."{{/if}}{{/if}}

ending.title: Housewarming
ending.epitaph: Here stood a welcome. It finally went home.

end_all_hallows.title: All Hallows
end_all_hallows.text:
The clock strikes, and your reflection gets up from its chair. It walks down the table with your walk and sits in Pip's place. The house counts, and the count is right.

You go out together through a door that stays open for one stroke of the bell. The street is two streets at once: wet leaves and a car alarm, and 1953, a privet hedge and a house with its porch light on. Pip lets go of the ribbon and runs up the path. The door opens before she reaches it. Just as it shuts, the light goes out.

You never see your own face again, in any glass.

ending.title: All Hallows
ending.epitaph: She left the light on. You never saw yourself again.

end_settled_account.title: Settled Account
end_settled_account.text:
Midnight finds you with your hands empty and nothing written against you, so the house has to bow. Mr. Marrow draws himself up to the whole of his eleven years and bows from the waist, and every stillness at the table bows with him. "Thank you for coming," he says. He does not say "Lovely." There is nothing to write down.{{#if ribbon}} At the threshold the ribbon in your hand goes slack.{{/if}}{{#if mirror}} In the dark glass of the front door, nobody walks out beside you.{{/if}}

You go down the path alone, past a jack-o'-lantern gone dark.{{#if name_given}} Every year after, a cream envelope comes in a careful schoolboy hand. *Do call again. —M.* You keep every one.{{/if}}

ending.title: Settled Account
ending.epitaph: Paid up, and politely shown out.

end_long_way_round.title: The Long Way Round
end_long_way_round.text:
The door opens as far as it must.{{#if ribbon}} At the top of the cellar stair the ribbon pulls once, back toward the table, and goes slack. The house counts heads, and you left no one in her place.{{/if}}{{#if candle}} You go up behind the honest flame through rooms that are only rooms: a hall, a stair, the front step, where the candle goes out.{{else}} Rooms stand back to let you pass, because his name asked them to.{{/if}} You ate nothing.{{#if debt>=1}} Nobody comes to close your page in the green book.{{else}} You owe nothing.{{/if}}{{#if mirror}} No window on the street gives you back.{{/if}}

{{#if true_name}}You are the only person alive who knows the name of the boy who keeps that house. Every Halloween you say it once, at 11:59, to nobody.{{else}}You get home late. Your mother says she waited up, and that is the last time anyone does. People are kind to you, and lend you umbrellas.{{/if}} Nobody, ever, asks you to stay for dinner.

ending.title: The Long Way Round
ending.epitaph: Never fed. Never kept. Never asked in.

end_head_count.title: Head Count
end_head_count.text:
Your reflection pulls out a chair at the long table, sits, and smooths the cloth with your hands. It does not look at you.

You hold up the candle and walk. By its light the stair is short and the hall is only a hall. Nobody stops you. A guest went down to the table and a guest is sitting at it, and the house does not look up.{{#if ribbon}} Halfway up, the ribbon in your hand goes slack, trailing back into the dark toward a chair with a cushion on it.{{else}} Behind you, every chair stays full.{{/if}} On the front step the candle goes out. Afterwards nothing shows you: not windows, not puddles, not the back of a spoon.

ending.title: Head Count
ending.epitaph: One went home. One stayed. Neither was all of you.

end_new_host.title: The New Host
end_new_host.text:
"Go," you tell him, by his name. "Get out."

Edwin takes off his gloves one finger at a time and lays them on the cloth, and shrugs out of his father's coat, and he is a thin boy in shirtsleeves with cork on his lip. He goes first through a doorway, for the first time in a hundred and twenty-eight years.

You turn to follow, and there is no way out that you can remember. Far above, someone knocks at the front door. The coat is nearly your size. Someone hands you the gloves. You put three sweets in a paper bag, and you hear yourself say, warmly, "Lovely."

ending.title: The New Host
ending.epitaph: Your host this evening, and every evening after.

end_every_day_november.title: Every Day Is November
end_every_day_november.text:
Between two strokes you slip out. Midnight does not let you go; it only fails to stop you. As the door closes Mr. Marrow says, "It comes due, you know."{{#if ribbon}} Pip's ribbon stays in your pocket, a promise with nowhere to go.{{/if}}

Outside it is the first of November: cold sun, white sky, jack-o'-lanterns going soft on every step. You go home and go to bed. You wake, and it is the first of November. The same pumpkins at the same stage of rot, the same bus, the same dog barking at it.{{#if mirror}} No shop window shows you.{{/if}} Everyone else grows older around you, politely, while you stay in one bright, cold, unending first of November.

ending.title: Every Day Is November
ending.epitaph: Got out on a technicality. Stayed out.

end_open_house.title: Open House
end_open_house.text:
You find the ring of the hatch under the cloth, and pull. You asked three times. It is only accepting.

It comes up slowly, the way a guest comes up a garden path, and it follows you home. It is very polite about it. It walks a little behind you, wearing your coat, and wipes its feet on your mat, and whoever opens your door says, without knowing why, "Well, come in, then." After that your house is warm. There is always something in the oven. The neighbours drop round, and stay, and stay. Everything smells, faintly, of warm bread and cloves.

ending.title: Open House
ending.epitaph: Something followed them home. It brought a casserole.

end_seat_at_table.title: Seat at the Table
end_seat_at_table.text:
You pick up your fork. It is the best thing you have ever tasted, and by the third mouthful you have stopped comparing it to anything, because there is nothing left to compare it with. There was a street once, and a voice calling you in. It goes the way breath goes off a window.

Mr. Marrow lays a gloved hand on the back of your chair. "Lovely," he says, and for once it means only that. Someone passes you the bread. The stillness in the next chair leans against your shoulder. You are very happy. You are part of the furniture now.

end_paid_in_full.title: Paid in Full

ending.title: Paid in Full
ending.epitaph: Settled with what was owed: everything.

end_strangers_wages.title: Stranger's Wages
end_strangers_wages.text:
You shove the chair back and run, down the long table, before the napkin has settled. The stillnesses turn their heads to watch you go.{{#if stance=treat}} "Then our guest is playing after all," Mr. Marrow says mildly.{{/if}}{{#if candle}} At the door the candle slips from your hand and is gone.{{/if}}

The cellar has never had a light in it. You find the shelves by touch, and the roots, which are warm. You cannot find the stair. Far behind you a boy's voice says, without any malice at all, "One to the house."{{#if stance=treat}} Nothing chases a guest. A guest leaves by the front door, and this is not it.{{else}}{{#if lies>=2}} It took more than one lie to make you a player, and he counted every one.{{else}}{{#if lied}} It took one lie to make you a player.{{/if}}{{/if}}{{/if}} The roots close round you, kindly, the way an armchair does.

ending.title: Stranger's Wages
ending.epitaph: Played the house. The house played back.
